name: The Central Limit Theorem
statement: Add up enough independent random things and their total is bell-shaped, whatever they were.
meaning: The central limit theorem says that the sum, or the average, of a large number of independent random variables with finite variance, suitably rescaled, approaches a normal — bell-shaped — distribution, no matter the shape of the distribution they came from. Aggregate enough small independent effects and the result is Gaussian. It is the reason the normal distribution turns up everywhere.
mechanism: Take independent, identically distributed variables with a finite mean and variance. Their average has mean equal to the common mean and variance equal to the common variance divided by the number of terms, so the average concentrates as the count grows. Rescale the deviation of the average from the mean by the square root of the count and, in the limit, its distribution converges to the standard normal. Crucially, the convergence is of the distribution of the sum or average, not of the individual values, and it holds whatever the underlying shape, provided no single term dominates.

examples.text: The total of a single die is flat across its faces, but the sum of many dice piles up into a bell curve — the theorem made visible.

The mean of a random sample, drawn again and again, distributes itself normally around the true mean even when the population is skewed, which is what lets statisticians build confidence intervals and tests.
Balls bouncing down a lattice of pegs, each nudged left or right at random, pile into a bell-shaped heap at the bottom — a physical demonstration going back to de Moivre and Laplace.

variants.name: The Lyapunov and Lindeberg forms
variants.text: Generalisations that drop the requirement of identical distribution, needing only independence and a condition ensuring no single term dominates the sum.

variants.name: The generalised central limit theorem
variants.text: The extension to infinite-variance variables, whose rescaled sums converge not to the normal but to a stable distribution, of which the Gaussian is the special case.

whyItMatters: It explains why the normal distribution is so pervasive — because so many quantities are sums of many small independent effects — and it is the theoretical foundation of statistical inference, underpinning the standard error, confidence intervals, and hypothesis tests. It is one of the central results of probability, the bridge from the behaviour of individual random quantities to the predictable shape of their aggregate.

working.text: look for bell-shaped distributions in sums and averages of many independent effects, whatever their individual shapes.
rely on the theorem to justify treating a sample mean as normally distributed with spread shrinking as the square root of the sample size.
before invoking it, confirm the variables are independent with finite variance and that none dominates the rest.

limits: The classical theorem requires finite variance: for heavy-tailed distributions like the Cauchy, which has no finite variance or even mean, it fails, and rescaled sums converge instead to a stable distribution. It requires independence, or at least weak dependence, and that no single term dominate. Convergence is not instant, and its speed, quantified by the Berry-Esseen theorem, depends on the distribution and the count; the common rule that a sample of thirty is always enough is a crude heuristic that fails for strongly skewed data.
misreadings: The theorem does not say the data themselves become normal as the sample grows — it concerns the distribution of the sum or average, not the individual observations. Nor does sampling any variable in large numbers yield a normal distribution; it applies to means and sums of independent draws. And thirty observations do not always suffice; that threshold has no general justification and can mislead badly for skewed distributions.
origin: Begun by Abraham de Moivre in 1733 for the binomial case and generalised by Laplace, then made rigorous by the Russian school of Chebyshev, Markov, and Lyapunov and by Lindeberg in the early twentieth century; the name central limit theorem is due to George Polya, around 1920.
